---

**Ancient Person of My Heart**

Ancient one, for whom I still
Spurn all flattering youth at will,
Mayst thou long escape old age's grip—
Aching, trembling, cold of lip;
But rest forever as thou art,
Ancient person of my heart.

Upon thy lips, though dry and worn,
Like furrows by the seasons torn,
I'll pour my kisses, warm and deep,
To wake the youth that lies asleep
(As gentle autumn rains recall
A second spring to bless it all);
Nor will I ever let thee part,
Ancient person of my heart.

That nobler part, which but to name
Would bring my sex a blush of shame,
Though held within age's frozen chain,
Shall from its icy grip be slain,
And by my healing touch restored,
Stand once again in strength adored.

All that a lover's heart could crave,
My love shall teach thee, constant, brave,
And for thy pleasure shall refine
Whatever art can lend to love divine.
Yet I shall love thee, free of art,
Ancient person of my heart.

---

# The Ancient Person of My Heart

Let others chase the smooth-cheeked youths who crowd
The halls of fashion, loud with empty praise—
I turn away from all that callow throng,
Their flattery a coin too cheaply made.
My heart has fixed itself upon one face,
Weathered and marked by time's unhurried hand,
And I proclaim without a shred of shame:
You are the ancient person of my heart.

Let no one tell you that the years have stolen
What once was yours; I will not have it so.
I wish you held forever at the hour
Before decline began its quiet theft,
Untouched by all the pains that old age brings—
The trembling hand, the dimming of the eye,
The frailty that creeps through failing bone.
Stay as you are, or let me hold you there
In memory's embrace, if flesh must fade.

And yet I will not simply mourn what's lost—
I mean to call it back with what I have:
My kisses, pressed upon your aged lips
Like rain that falls upon the autumn ground,
Not to conclude the season but begin
A second spring, unlooked-for and more sweet
For coming after harvest, after frost.
So let my mouth upon your mouth restore
Some portion of the fire that time has banked,
And prove that autumn, too, can bloom again.

I vow to you, though vigor may have fled
And left you feeling frozen in its grip,
That tenderness can thaw what years have bound.
Your manhood, which you fear has slipped away
Into the cold indifference of age,
I mean to summon back with patient care—
Not through deception, not through forced pretense,
But through the honest labor of desire
That does not measure worth by youth alone.

And though I own I use what arts I know—
The practiced touch, the words that stoke desire,
The small deceptions pleasure sometimes needs—
Let no one doubt the truth beneath these acts:
My love itself contains no artifice.
Whatever skill I bring to serve our joy,
The heart that offers it is wholly true,
And what I feel for you, though dressed in craft,
Remains, at core, as honest as the dawn.

# On the Restoration of Love in Age

## An Expansion Upon a Poem Attributed to the Earl of Rochester

There exists, among the works ascribed to John Wilmot, Earl of Rochester—that most audacious and paradoxical voice of Restoration verse—a poem of curious tenderness, one that stands apart from his more notorious satires and bawdy provocations. This piece, addressed to an aged lover, constructs its meaning through a sustained juxtaposition of decay and renewal, deploying the vocabulary of winter and death—"withered," "frozen," the imagery of frost upon the bough—only to counter each image of ruin with an assertion of restorative power drawn not from artifice, but from the authentic force of devoted feeling.

The poem's central conceit operates through paradox: the body may bear the marks of time's passage, the flesh may seem frost-bound and diminished, yet the speaker insists that these very signs of decay are not final. Rather than treating age as an insurmountable barrier to desire, the verse proposes that genuine affection possesses an almost alchemical capacity to reverse what time has wrought. The withered may bloom again; the frozen may thaw. This is not achieved through cosmetic pretense or the superficial charms that typically govern courtship poetry of the era—the powdered wig, the painted cheek, the practiced flattery of youth—but through something the speaker frames as more elemental and true: the natural, artless expression of physical and emotional intimacy.

This distinction matters considerably. Rochester's broader corpus is often preoccupied with the gap between appearance and reality, between the performed self and the authentic body beneath its social costume. Here, that preoccupation takes a gentler turn. The poem seems to argue that love's rejuvenating power is most potent precisely when stripped of pretense—when it operates through direct, unmediated devotion rather than the elaborate courtly rituals that Restoration society prized. The lover's youth is not restored by disguising age but by the transformative energy of being genuinely desired and touched.

In this sense, the poem articulates what might be called a radical theory of desire—one that refuses the conventional hierarchy privileging youthful beauty as the sole legitimate object of erotic attention. Instead, it suggests that desire itself, when sufficiently sincere and sufficiently embodied, can transcend the biological realities of aging. The ravages of time become, within the poem's logic, not an ending but merely a condition to be answered—and possibly reversed—through the sustained force of physical and emotional devotion.

Such a vision fits uneasily, yet meaningfully, within Rochester's larger poetic project. Where his satires often expose the futility of desire, the emptiness of court life, or the body's inevitable betrayal by disease and decay, this poem offers something closer to consolation—a suggestion that even as the body fails, love itself might remain a force capable of working against nature's own decree, restoring warmth to what has gone cold, and vigor to what the years have taken.

# The Weight of Ancient Wisdom

Throughout **all** of human history, we have looked backward to move forward. The **ancient** civilizations—Sumer, Egypt, China, the Indus Valley—built not just monuments of stone, but foundations of thought that have endured across an extraordinarily **long** span of time.

Consider how the wisdom of these early societies still echoes in our daily lives. The mathematical principles discovered by ancient Babylonian scholars remain valid in **all** modern engineering. The philosophical questions posed by ancient Greek thinkers continue to shape debates that have persisted for millennia—questions about justice, truth, and the nature of existence that show no signs of being resolved anytime soon.

What makes **ancient** knowledge so remarkable is its resilience. Despite wars, natural disasters, and the slow erosion of time, fragments of wisdom have survived a **long** journey through history to reach us today. Clay tablets, papyrus scrolls, oral traditions passed from generation to generation—**all** of these served as vessels carrying human understanding forward.

Yet perhaps the most profound lesson from **ancient** times is this: civilizations rise and fall, but the human spirit's curiosity, creativity, and desire to understand the world remains constant. **All** peoples, in **all** corners of the earth, throughout the **long** arc of history, have grappled with the same fundamental questions—where do we come from, why are we here, and what happens when we're gone?

In studying the **ancient** past, we don't merely satisfy historical curiosity. We connect with something larger than ourselves—a **long**, unbroken thread of human experience that links us to **all** who came before, and will link us to **all** who come after.
